tainly do not take any offence to it whatever. The question helps me if the Chair will give me time to answer it.
I see possibilities for industrial Cape Breton, and indeed for the whole of Atlantic Canada, but that has to be done with the help of both provincial and federal Governments. Referring to doom and gloom, the doom and gloom represents what we see Governments doing on behalf of Atlantic Canada. If we see there is hope and Governments are sincere about helping us, then there will not be the feeling of doom and gloom. Goodness knows, people in Atlantic Canada and industrial Cape Breton could not have carried on without that hope and without feeling there would be a better time. The problem is that industrial development is competitive.
Recently Pratt & Whitney announced that it was going to Halifax. If someone had said to Pratt & Whitney, "You have to go to industrial Cape Breton," that company would have said no. What should be done? Would that mean you would give them all the money they needed to go to industrial Cape Breton? The answer is no. One has to look at the situation as one aspect. We have to encourage industry. We have to tell industry that industry will be successful there and that there is a good industrial framework. As part of that framework one must co-ordinate all departments, both provincially and federally, so that one hand is not doing something contrary to what the other hand wants done. One must not reduce transportation facilities that will be needed for the industrial possibilities which the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and the Department of Development in Nova Scotia feel will be necessary to entice development. They have to work together and co-ordinate. You have to have the infrastructure in a community that people need. You have to have schools and hospitals that meet what the people want. That is part of regional development. You have to have downtown facilities that are not elaborate but a conceptual idea of what you are going to develop in that community. Then the people who locate and live there will see this as a community that is being planned for a positive future.
Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Justice and Attorney
General of Canada): Mr. Speaker, I am glad that this motion has been moved so that we can produce some facts to show what has been done for Atlantic Canada. However, I have had the unfortunate experience of listening to two discourses which really make one despair.
When I listened to the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan), I thought to myself of an old song. To paraphrase that old song, it goes, "Oh, Russell, I hardly knew you". Where was all this passion, emotion and disgust a year ago? After all, it was the Liberal Party, which that hon. gentleman represents, that was in power for the last 20 years while these conditions that he described were allowed to arise in Cape Breton. The Hon. Member himself has been here for the last four or five years. Everything he said today about Cape Breton was just as true a year ago, and nothing was done about it. The situation was allowed to worsen and to worsen by

that Government and that Hon. Member. Yet we heard him today, and all we could think was: What a fine actor. They are marvels at spurious indignation. Where was that indignation last year? They are marvels at hypocritical alarm, carefully constructed crocodile tears, yowling, howling, bawling and mewling; not policy, puling, drooling, hoping to fool them. We did not hear one suggestion from the hon. gentleman about what should be done to help Cape Breton or the unemployed, or what this Government should have done over the last 20 years. It was like the wind whistling through a whale's spout and just as useful. The hon. gentleman was not even as useful and did not make as much sense as a blow-hole of a whale would have made. I have heard many whales through their blow-holes. They were all more interesting, made more sense, had more logic and wasted less time than did the hon. gentleman in his speech in the House, and they would have been a lot more effective.
Patriotism used to be described as the last refuge of the scoundrel, but it is not patriotism any longer. It is spurious indignation, hypocritical alarm, and the kind of unctuous bunkum and mind-boggling blarney we have heard for the last 40 minutes from the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys and the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon).
I have more sympathy for the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor. He was never in power, so he cannot be held responsible. Of course the NDP is completely irresponsible. Its members have never been in power. They are never going to be in power. They can whistle and blow through their blow-holes until kingdom come; they will never be asked to account for the nonsense they get on with or for the promises they make.
The people of Ontario, sophisticated as they are, know that. That is why they only gained two members in that deluge yesterday. They only swelled their ranks by two. The Liberals are much better at fooling the people of Ontario than is the NDP. The NDP, having no responsibility and never having to be accountable for anything, could only increase its number of members in Ontario by two. That says a great deal for the educational system of Ontario. But the educational system in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island is much better because we only have, I think it is, two provincial Members for the Atlantic provinces who represent the NDP. Of course it was a magnificent victory! I remember they had one Member in the Newfoundland House. The election was called last March and they have one Member now, and they declared a great victory. Isn't it marvellous? Last year we had the federal election and they came back with fewer Members than they had before, and that was announced as a great victory. The only Party in history that cheers loudly when it loses Members is the NDP. It is the NDP nirvana, pedal power, the never-never pills which the NDP offers to the people of Cape Breton. The people of Cape Breton are not interested. They are not interersted in never-never solutions from never-never people who will never, never be in power. The NDP is the only group in this House which does not need drugs to suffer from fantasies.
Let us get down to business here. Let us forget the socialist slops and their Marxist mythology, their pseudo solutions, the detritus of dismal ditties from dotty dodos, and get on to some facts here. I will only deal with my own Province of Newfoundland and Labrador. I will not deal with the whole Atlantic area, and I will not deal with just my own district because there is very little done in my district. I am always sacrificing for the other districts down in Newfoundland and Labrador. That is what happens in St. John's West. However, in this little list I have here, there are one or two things which are being done, even in St. John's West.
Let us look at this resolution. What a joke! Thank heavens the person who moved it, the Hon. Member for Gander-Twil-lingate (Mr. Baker), is now coming back into the House to take his medicine. The resolution reads:
That this House condemns the Government for its indifference and negligence toward Atlantic Canada, especially with regard to regional industrial developments, fisheries and transportation.
It is a motion moved by a Member of the last administration-he had the gall to move this-an administration which declared war on the Atlantic provinces, which savagely attacked and savaged its own provincial administration in Newfoundland for the last 8 or 10 years, which refused to sign an offshore oil and gas agreement, which tried to grind them down, which went down to Newfoundland and refused to sign agreements in the Confederation Building, the headquarters of the Newfoundland Government. The Liberals said: "You come down and sign them here in the Hotel Newfoundland where we the great, mighty federal Government are". That is the way the Liberals treated Newfoundland, and now they condemn this Government for indifference and negligence toward Atlantic Canada.
Why do they think they are out on their what-nots? It is because of their indifference and their neglect toward Atlantic Canada and toward the rest of Canada that they are out on their what-nots. I could spell what-not, but it would probably be unparliamentary. It is the only three-letter word which 1 know that might be unparliamentary.
Let me give a little list. The Atlantic Accord-if nothing else was ever done by the administration of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in Atlantic Canada or in Newfoundland or Labrador, the Atlantic Accord would make up for everything else, everything else.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is $225 million of the $300 million fund. It is not a loan, it is a grant. Is this indifference and neglect? Is establishing the principle that revenue sharing shall be on the same basis as it is between Canada and other provinces indifference or neglect toward Atlantic Canada? How can the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate move such a resolution with that background? This one agreement alone means that Newfoundland will be able to establish and collect revenues from offshore oil and gas as though it was under the land in Alberta. Is that indifference and neglect? No, that is being saved from the indifference and neglect of the last seven or eight years.
I would not mind if this resolution had been moved by the NDP. I cannot blame its members for anything. In fact, some of them are perfectly likable. It is just like members of your family-you think they are useless but they are very likable because they are related to you and, after all, you can choose your friends but you cannot choose all the members of your family. That is the way I look upon NDP Members. They are perfectly likable, even though some of them are not all that useful, but we cannot hold them responsible. They have never been in power. They did not grind Newfoundland down. They did not say no to regional development. They did not take away the self-respect of Newfoundlanders. They did not tell Newfoundlanders that they were not as good as other people across the country and, therefore, could not be trusted to look after their own resources.
The NDP has never done that, but the Liberal Party has. The Party which the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate represents has done that. He stood by in this House year after year and let them do it. Now he has the gall, the crass hypocrisy, to move this silly jejune-you see I am bilingual- resolution about indifference and negligence towards Atlantic Canada.
I have to watch the clock. I will have to skip quickly. I cannot go into detail. The Canada-Newfoundland roads agreement to the tune of $180 million was agreed to in March. That
Supply
is to be spent by the federal Government and the Newfoundland Government jointly on the Trans-Canada Highway on roads in Labrador and on the Avalon Peninsula over the next five to six years. That is the biggest roads agreement ever entered into between the two Governments. Is that indifference and neglect, especially with regard to transportation? Is this Member in the real world? Does he not know what is going on around him? When he gets in his car in the Town of Gander, he is right on the Trans-Canada Highway where $180 million will be spent, and he says there is indifference and neglect. What does he want? Is $180 million not enough?
Let me just list a few of the other things that have been done with respect to Newfoundland in seven months.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I wonder if the Minister would care to clarify something. Is he telling us now that Cabinet and Treasury Board have approved $180 million for Newfoundland? I know he announced that during the campaign. Little good it did him, but he announced it during the campaign. Is he telling us that he has Cabinet and Treasury Board approval and a signed agreement to spend $180 million? I just want the record to be straight. I think the record should be set straight.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret to inform the Hon. Member that that is not a point of order. That is debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me set the Hon. Member's mind at ease. I have done what he could not do in four or five years. Yes, Treasury Board has approved it. Yes, the Cabinet has approved it. The agreement will be signed in the next couple of weeks. The work will go forward this year. Nothing to it. You just need to have a Government that is interested in helping the province.
I did not want to embarrass the Hon. Member, but now that he has annoyed me, I will. In the pulp and paper agreement, signed December 20, 1984, the federal share will be $38.5 million and the total will be $46.3 million. Of the $180 million highways' agreement, $12 million will come from the federal Government of Canada. That will be the federal contribution. We are only getting started.
Earlier in 1984, as the election date came closer, the federal Government at last signed some agreements-planning, mineral development, Burin Peninsula, rural development, ocean industries, and tourism. Those agreements were signed by the federal Liberal Government after holding off for a year and a half, bullying and punishing and trying to do all it could to damage the Newfoundland Government. They were signed as the election came on in the futile hope they could save some of their seats.
And we did.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They saved the hon. gentleman, but he is on a hair's breadth, he is gone the next time. That totals $77.85 million which the federal Government will contribute under those agreements. What about the two agreements that we agreed to in the last seven months? The federal contributions

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I just told the Hon. Member it was approved by Treasury Board and approved by the Cabinet. All we have to do is to list it now and scratch our names on it. We will probably go to Newfoundland to do that so that we can be sure that the hon. gentleman and everybody else will know that it has been done. Is that negligence, neglect or indifference?
I am not sure how much time I have left. I will have to go very rapidly to put the nails into the coffin of this silly resolution, this jejune resolution, this careless resolution, this negligent resolution, this grossly negligent resolution, this conscienceless resolution, this resolution of which the hon. gentleman should be ever ashamed. It is in the same league as the resolution that was moved by Mr. Pearson years ago when the PCs got in for the first time in years and he moved that they get out and turn the Government over to the Liberals. This is the kind of resolution that this is.
Modernization of the Corner Brook mill, the Grand Falls pulp and paper mills, is a $37 million modernization program, with $5.6 million coming from the federal Government. The Marystown offshore service facility, an $11 million agreement, was signed on September 28, 1984. The Cow Head facility near Marystown involves a $7.7 million grant from DRIE. I could go on and on, Mr. Speaker. There is the freezing of container rates. This motion speaks of indifference and negligence.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Let the record show that the Marystown funds came out of the Burin Penninsula fund, which was signed when we were the Government of Canada. Let the record be straight.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is not a point of order, unfortunately.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that the Hon. Member does not know the rules. They were never in the House when they were in Government, so he is not familiar with the rules. It is not a point of order. There is the freezing of container rates on Terra Transport where we took action a couple of months ago to see that the container rates were not increased as the CTC directed. We are continuing assistance to the Ace Shipping Company while that proceeds. Is that indifference or neglect? Then there is the St. John's Convention Centre. I know the Hon. Member hates to have anything go near St. John's. We know the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) was an enemy of St. John's and anything that came near St. John's. He did everything he could to keep everything away from St. John's. There was the agreement on the St. John's Convention Centre. The cost will be $7 million, of which DRIE is putting in $1.7 million.
There are the Town of Channel-Port aux Basques water supply facilities. The Hon. Member tried to cod the people of
Port aux Basques that they were going to pay for a water supply system, but he did nothing about it. At last, after months of effort, I have $6.5 million from the Government to construct the new water system at Channel-Port aux Basques. Is that indiffernece? Is that neglect? My God, it's a miracle. There was also the combined services building at St. John's airport.
With regard to search and rescue, for years hon. gentlemen opposite were satisfied with inadequate search and rescue facilities on the east coast of Newfoundland. They did nothing. It did not matter what happened, what disaster struck or occurred. They sat on their big red what-nots and did nothing. They think they can pass a resolution here saying that we are showing indifference and negligence toward Atlantic Canada when we have improved immensely the search and rescue capability in St. John's and for the offshore with a second fixed-wing tracker aircraft, with two long-range DND aircraft and an additional helicopter based in St. John's. I do not have the time to go into all of the capability that has been assembled for offshore search and rescue work in connection with the offshore development. They want us to pass a resolution saying that we showed indifference and negligence. Why should we pass a resolution in the face of one or all the things I have mentioned, much less all of them?
There is the new Challenge '85 program. Yes, there is an unemployment problem in Newfoundland, but the people of Newfoundland know that the NDP is never going to resolve it. NDP Members can go down and look sympathetic and concerned, and I hope they are sympathetic and concerned, but Newfoundlanders know the NDP will never never be doing anything about it. We are attempting to do something about it. We have a Challenge '85 program, not only to give young people jobs in the summer, but to give them experience so that they can have jobs for the rest of their lives, so that they can develop their skills and receive training. We are taking a long-range view, not the short-range political, putrid view that the hon. gentlemen opposite had over their 20 years in office. That is not indifference and negligence, but concern for people, concern for young people. We are starting to take action that will do something about it, not as the jackanapes opposite who did nothing about it.
In Goose Bay, in the hon. gentleman's district, we are going to do something. We are going to save Goose Bay. We are going to revitalize it. The North Warning System is going to help Goose Bay and help the whole of Labrador. There will be a magnificent increase in defence spending in Labrador. The hon. gentleman's Party objects to it, fights against it and quarrels. With regard to the star wars' Member in the first row, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), I say that star wars for him is a knock between the eyes. That will give him star wars. The Hon. Member is objecting to all of this that will help build up Labrador and the Goose Bay air base. He just sits there and lets his colleagues object to that. They object to the three long-range radar stations for the Labrador coast, the Baffin Peninsula area and the other area that will be part of that system. In the next few

years, $395 million will be spent in Labrador and along the Baffin Peninsula area. I do not have time to go into the details of it all but there are other plans for the Goose Bay area.
The Hon. Member should come over here to join us. I will make him welcome. He is a decent enough chap. However, his views have been obscured by his years in the Liberal Party. We will make him welcome and I think we can help him along.
There is a Canada Works special allocation of $6 million in connection with needs related to the fisheries. The Placentia Nursing Home will be built in my own district. There will be $18 million spent on a Winter Canada Works Program. At the Memorial University, there will be a grant for work-term students that will help 72 students. speechtext: I could go on and on but I am delighted to be here today to speak again about the incipient hypocrisy of the motion moved by the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate. Mr. Speaker, after that I do not know whether I should ask a question or simply make a comment. I was wondering if I did all that the Hon. Minister claims I did.
The Hon. Minister mentioned bullying. I suppose the biggest bully in this Chamber, when it comes to making sure that projects go to his riding, is the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). Most people who observe the actions of this Government would believe that Newfoundland stops at the St. John's overpass.
The other day I heard the Minister say that there would be international flights into the City of St. John's. How can the Minister of Justice say that when there is a procedure that must be followed? Having international flights into St. John's must be approved by the CTC, the Customs Department, Transport Canada and ICAO. The Minister knows that, but he publicly states that those international flights that are passing through Gander will pass through the City of St. John's. How can he state publicly to the people of Newfoundland that flights will be taken from the Town of Gander and given to the City of St. John's?
While the Minister is answering that question, perhaps he could tell us how the Atlantic Accord can be such a magnificent document when a section of that Accord indicates that no industrial use will be made of offshore oil in Newfoundland until the industrial capacity of eastern Canada is satisfied?

This is fine for Petromont in the Speaker's riding. It is certainly fine for the ridings of some other Hon. Members of the House. Perhaps that was the intent of the Accord. However, how does the Minister justify that? It is a good thing that Accord was called the Atlantic Accord because it could not have been called the Newfoundland Accord. Perhaps the Minister could make reference to that.
The Minister spoke of search and rescue helicopters. Do you know where those search and rescue helicopters came from, Mr. Speaker? They came from Gander and are going to the riding of the Hon. Minister. Those helicopters came from the search and rescue facilities based in the Town of Gander in order to serve all of the province. Those facilities were placed there by the former Liberal administration. It is not unusual for this Minister to take those helicopters into his own riding. As far as the hon. gentleman is concerned, Newfoundland stops at the St. John's overpass.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad the Hon. Member rose to ask those fuddling questions. He has given me a chance to deal with them.
Let us first deal with the overpass. The Hon. Member is talking in local terms. By that, he means that everything is done in St. John's and nothing happens outside of St. John's. Let us just look at what is taking place. There will be a $180 million Canada-Newfoundland roads agreement. Not one cent of that will be spent in the City of St. John's. It will all be spent on roads in Labrador and the southern Avalon Peninsula. Then there is the modernization of the Corner Brook mill. Is Corner Brook in St. John's? Of course not; it is on the west coast of Newfoundland. The Grand Falls pulp and paper mill will be receiving $33 million. That is in Grand Falls. Marystown will be getting $11 million. Not one cent, one nickel or one dime of that will be going to St. John's. I am the most unselfish son of a gun I have ever come across when it comes to my own district.
The only thing here that is designed specifically for St. John's is the St. John's Convention Centre. That is in St. John's but one cannot have a St. John's Convention Centre if it is not in St. John's. We had to put that in St. John's. After all, it is the capital of Newfoundland and it is the biggest city in Newfoundland. It is called the St. John's Convention Centre so we had to put it in St. John's. It is too bad we could not put it in Gander. However, if it is to be called the St. John's Convention Centre, it has to be put in St. John's. The Newfoundland Government has helped Gander with its convention facilities and has recently given the hotel there help.
The money that would be provided for the Town of Channel-Port aux Basques water supply facilities will not be provided to St. John's. It is going to Channel-Port aux Basques. Where was the Hon. Member when I read this list?
Regarding search and rescue, there was a helicopter moved from Gander to St. John's because the offshore industry is off St. John's, not off Gander. When there is an emergency in the

May 3, 1985
Supply
offshore, the helicopter will be 160 miles closer to the disaster and will be able to get there considerably earlier. That helicopter should have been moved years ago, but the hon. gentleman selfishly kept it in Gander despite the fact that it should have been close to the offshore area. That kind of political willfulness and disregard of the health and safety of people in the offshore has now been stopped.
The North Warning System that will be updated in Goose Bay is not in St. John's. A few of the Canada Works programs will be in St. John's, but the Placentia Nursing Home is not in St. John's. I could go on and on. That deals with that part of the question.
Regarding international flights into Gander, only two or three trans-Atlantic flights that go from Newfoundland to the United Kingdom are being moved. Air Canada now uses Gander despite the fact that the traffic originates in St. John's, the Avalon Peninsula and the Burin Peninsula. The rights of the travelling public have been forgotten. The extra expenses incurred by the 60 per cent or 70 per cent of the travelling public who come from those areas are ignored because of the political willfulness and selfishness of the hon. gentleman. Moving these flights will not harm Gander in the least. The airport in Gander will remain an international airport. No other flights will be moved.
Air Canada wants to operate flights from the St. John's airport because the travelling public originates there. Air Canada wants to save the travelling public many dollars and wants to save them the aggravation of trying to get to Gander where they wait hour after hour to get an international flight to the United Kingdom. Gander will not suffer but, for a change, the travelling public will be taken into consideration. The hon. gentleman's selfish willfulness will no longer prevent us from doing what should have been done, 8, 10 or 12 years ago.
Have 1 dealt with it all? Is there anything else I can deal with that might be on the hon. gentleman's mind? Much will remain where it is. No one in St. John's wants to take anything away from Gander. However, where there is an obvious need for the travelling public to be served so that they can be saved money, time and inconvenience, then surely something should be done. Narrow political parochialism and selfishness should not stop that from being done. I can assure the hon gentleman that Gander is not going to suffer as a result of that action, and as long as I am in the Government of Canada, Gander will not suffer at all.
Mr. Speaker, as a new Member I have to say it is a magnificent experience to listen to the Hon. Minister.
Hear, hear!

It indicates to us how sadly confined he is in the Ministry of Justice. However, I did want to indicate that although I am impressed with the impact of the Newfoundland education system in teaching people how to speak, I am not so impressed with how they teach them to count. At last count
there were six provincial New Democrat Members in Atlantic Canada and growing fast.
I am struck as well by the comment about the New Democrats as a never-never Party. I suppose it is preferable to be accused of never doing anything because you are not in power rather than being accused of never doing anything when you are in power. The Minister should, now that it is eight months since the Cabinet was formed, start to deal with the reality that his Government is in power. It is no longer enough to blame on the past what is happening today in Atlantic Canada. It is important for this Minister to recognize that he is in power, the Government is in power, and it has the potential to act. If it is a choice between being perfectly likable or jejune, or magnificently preposterous, perhaps being perfectly likable is preferable.
The Minister has talked about things increasing in Atlantic Canada. The main thing that has increased in Atlantic Canada since this Government came to power is the unemployment rate, and I think it is time this Government recognized that and did something about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is hard to get a question out of what the hon. gentleman said, but we know we are in power. We know that is the reality. Did I not just give a list of the results of our being in power for just one province of Canada, and a small one at that? Yes, we are in power and we are doing something. We are taking a long-term approach. The Challenge '85 program, for which the provinces have been looking for years, will not only give people short-term jobs but will help them in their future careers. That is being in power. We knew the reality of being in power when the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) restored VIA Rail services. The people of Canada know the reality that we are in power. The people of Newfoundland know it because they are treated like decent human beings for a change. They get some respect, they are not treated as they were in the old days. They know, because of the Atlantic Accord, that we are in power. We know the reality because we put forward the Atlantic Accord and the Western Accord. The Hon. Member from Alberta knows we are in power and what the reality is because we got the energy problems settled in western Canada. The people in Quebec know we are in power because of the things we have been doing in Quebec.
We know the reality that we are in power, and we are going to take a long-term approach. We know how bad unemployment is. I live in Newfoundland, I have lived there all my life and I intend to continue living there all my life and I know what unemployment is like in Cape Breton. We know it is not easy to beat that. We do not even know if we are going to be able to beat it, but we are going to take a better crack at it than has been taken before because we are going to go at it in a long-term way, not just for the immediate quick fix. That is the kind of approach that we and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) are taking.
Yes, the reality is that we are in power. We know it, the people of Canada know it, and we are not going to forget it. The Member is not going to forget it either because with the
May 3, 1985

kind of caterwauling performance we have had today we can see that they are on the road to ruin and perdition. They are going nowhere if they continue this way over the next four years, so keep it up.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) said that the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) was a man of humour. He may very well be, but he is not accurate and he does not enjoy stating the facts as they should be. The fact is that what he has said here today is completely inaccurate, not factual, not the truth. I had intended to talk about issues which I thought were of serious concern in Atlantic Canada, but of necessity I have to deal with the points made by the Hon. Member for St. John's West.
First he says that the Atlantic Accord, if nothing else is done by his Government-and so far nothing else has been done by his Government-would make up for everything else. Well, we may get $200 million a year in a few years' time if the Hibernia project goes ahead. I hope it does. But after all the profits and all the taxes all we may get is $200 million a year. Our deficit now is $300 million. The Hon. Member says the Atlantic Accord is going to make up for everything, and that is the first inaccuracy.
He then went on to name all the agreements which his Government has signed. There has been one agreement signed by that Party since they became the Government of Canada, and that is money we put aside for the Port aux Basques water system. They get Cable TV down in Port aux Basques and Corner Brook, and they know the accuracy of what I am saying now. We met with the Port aux Basques Town Council and the Development Association and agreed to set aside $6.5 million for their water system when we were the Government of Canada. That is the agreement and the only agreement that Party has signed since they became the Government of Canada. Apart from the announcement, not a signed agreement, the $180 million for roads, which we will not see this year because it is too late for the construction season anyway, all other agreements were signed when we were the Government of Canada.
He talked about nothing going into St. John's. The Music School, which agreement we signed when we were the Government, is in St. John's in the Hon. Member's riding. The Fisheries College, $47 million, is in St. John's, in the Hon. Member's riding, and the agreement was signed and it was put there when we were the Government of Canada. There is a convention centre in St. John's. The Minister of Development for Newfoundland cannot deny this because it is a matter of record; we had agreed to that when we were the Government of Canada. So those three projects in St. John's were agreed to and most of the money provided when we were the Government of Canada.
The Hon. Member went through a lot of other agreements such as the Ocean Industries agreement. That was signed when we were the Government of Canada, between January and June of 1984, involving a total of $28 million. There was an agreement on tourism, a total of $14.7 million, signed when

we were the Government of Canada. A planning agreement worth $4 million was signed when we were the Government. The minerals agreement is worth $21.95 million. We had the Burin Peninsula development agreement-and this is where he plays fast and loose with the fact-and that was signed when we were the Government of Canada, for a total of $28 million. The new mine at St. Lawrence came out of that same fund. This is a matter of record so let us set the record straight and not play fast and loose with the facts.
There was a rural development agreement involving a total of $18.2 million, signed with Newfoundland when we were the Government of Canada. He talked about the pulp and paper agreement, and that also was signed when we were the Government. He may have enlarged it, he may have put some more money into that agreement, but it was signed when we were the Government of Canada.
These are the facts and I do not think the Minister of Justice should be allowed to get away with that nonsense in this House, to get away with trying to fool people and mislead the House and the people of Newfoundland into thinking that his Government has suddenly, out of the blue, done something for our province which had not been done before. That is not the case. I think the people of Newfoundland have shown that they know that was not the case.
This morning the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) talked about the people's knowledge of the Liberal record. In the federal election the people of Newfoundland gave the Liberal Party popular support equivalent to that given to the Liberal Party in the Province of Ontario last night. Three of us sit in this chamber now as living proof that the people of Newfoundland know what the Liberal Government did for them. They returned us here because of that.
The Minister speaks of Goose Bay. They spent $2 million to improve a communication system in Goose Bay that is not going to create one single job there. I wish he had risen today in the House and said that his Government was going to create the NATO training base that we have been asking for. That would create jobs. So far the Government has not created one single job in Goose Bay. It must be done, but it has not done it so far. Do not allow them to mislead the House on that as well.
The Minister talked about search and rescue. He talked about taking a helicopter from Gander and putting it where the need was greatest. Seventy per cent of all the marine accidents along the northeast coast of Newfoundland occur within the range of Gander. The Hon. Member has oil on his mind. He is like Premier Peckford who, during the election campaign, bragged about the agreements that we had signed. The Premier of Newfoundland, who almost lost that election, never mentioned the Atlantic Accord during that election campaign, but he did mention those agreements which were signed. That is a case on which the record must be set straight.
The Hon. Member said the helicopter was taken from Gander and put in St. John's because that is where the traffic is. That is not the case. The traffic is off the northeast coast of

Newfoundland. The Hon. Member is going to rue the day when a tragedy happens in that area and the aircraft is not there to take care of it. I agree that there must be increased capability in St. John's for the oil rigs, but the companies must take their responsibility too. The Government of Canada has a responsibility for the fishing craft as well as for the oil rigs. That is why it should have maintained the helicopter in Gander to do the job that was necessary. It has not put anything new there. It has only re-allocated resources. That is not a step in the right direction.
The Minister spoke about Challenge '85. Nineteen hundred applications have been received in Newfoundland under Challenge '85. Twenty per cent of those are career related. They talk about the great use which the public sector is going to make of this. The public sector is not making use of it and neither are the municipalities. The municipalities are being forced to put money which they do not have into Challenge '85. The municipalities of Newfoundland find themselves very hard pressed indeed.
Under Summer Canada the municipalities were given funds free and clear. Federal funds created jobs for young people. This year the municipalities are being forced to contribute 25 per cent of the cost of creating those summer jobs. As a consequence, there will not be as many jobs as there were last year. I do not believe there will be that many created by the private sector either because small companies in Newfoundland do not have the 50 per cent which is needed under Challenge '85. 1 do not think that Challenge '85 will work out as well as the Hon. Member thinks it will. My main concern is the way in which the Hon. Member has misled the House. I believe that the record must be put straight.
I would like to go on to other things which I think must be done. The Minister did not really address the problem of regional development this morning. We talked about this in relation to the Investment Canada Bill. I have seen nothing so far to tell us that the Government in power has any policy for directing funds or employment to the regions of Canada which are in most need, such as the Atlantic region. I could point to the things which have been done away with. The Atlantic provinces have been seriously affected by that. I would like to read from an editorial in the January 3 Telegraph Journal. It reads:
Prime Minister Brian Mulroney and his deficit-slashing Finance Minister, Michael Wilson, would be well advised to take a second look at any schemes that would scale down Ottawa's involvement in regional economic development in Canada.
In setting out to cut spending, the new Government evidently sees a scenario in which the federal Government would reduce its role in direct stimulation of economic growth in various regions and look to the private sector to help fill the
gap-
But the problem in regions such as the Atlantic Provinces is the private sector's limited ability to generate more growth under present conditions.
Thomas Maxwell, chief economist for the Conference Board of Canada, points out quite correctly that Atlantic Canada is a region in which the private sector lacks the resources to fill the inevitable void that would be created if Ottawa were to cut back on its support and assistance.
That is an accurate description of what is happening. While it may be true that there are parts of the country where the
private sector can carry the load, the Atlantic region is not one of them. The Government has not realized that by indiscriminately cutting programs across Canada it has hurt underdeveloped regions where the private sector is not strong enough to stand on its own feet and will not be strong enough unless something is done, and it will not be done quickly. It has not realized that through indiscriminate cutting it has hurt the Atlantic area.
There is a whole list of examples of the kind of thing the Telegraph Journal is talking about in its editorial. For example, there has been a $250 million reduction in PIP grants for the offshore. We have not yet been told what will be put in its place. There has been a $11.7 million reduction in capital expenditures in the fisheries development program. Marketing and the small craft harbours program was cut. There was a reduction in non-profit and co-op housing. That is not simply a matter of housing for people. That means that a lot of small businesses such as construction firms and lumber yards in the Atlantic Provinces will be very severely hurt as a result of that cut-back in housing.
This morning the Minister talked about what he was doing for the Atlantic Provinces. One thing he did was to cut tourism out of the IRDP program altogether. I think that tourism is going to be a sunrise industry in the Atlantic Provinces and it cannot now qualify for any grants under the Industrial Regional Development Program. There is a water slide in a town in my constituency which is attracting a great many tourists. It is a good, imaginative idea of a small businessman that is working well. It is making money and attracting people to that area. That kind of thing can no longer be done because tourism is no longer eligible under the IRDP.
Another thing which has been cut is ferry service. There are ferries along the northeast coast of Newfoundland, the coast of Labrador, and the south coast that have been cut. All of these things will have a very severe impact in Atlantic Canada and Newfoundland. We do not have a healthy private sector which can take up the slack. Perhaps Toronto, parts of Alberta and parts of British Columbia can do that, but that type of indiscriminate cutting will hurt people in the Atlantic provinces where the economy is not strong enough to stand on its own two feet. That is starting to happen now. The Atlantic Accord will not take up the slack.
What will we do in Newfoundland for the next five or ten years until all the money rolls in from the oil? How do we feed our people and get jobs in the meantime? What is the Government going to do in regional economic policy? That is a serious question which deserves to be answered but has not yet been answered. I hope there are some answers in the Budget when it comes down.
I have some questions for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). I have some positive suggestions of things that could be done. Let me tell the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) what can be done in Goose Bay. I hope he will take it up with the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen). Let us not talk about star wars because that will not create jobs. Let us talk about a NATO training base where the Government could
May 3, 1985

make money and attract foreign companies to Goose Bay, as it is doing now, so the Government of Canada would make money. They would be paying guests in our country. I suggest that a proposal for a NATO training base in Goose Bay would not only keep our NATO commitment-

speechtext: Why didn't you do it?

We did it. We signed an agreement with the West Germans and with the British. We have the Americans there. We started it, you go farther and create a NATO training base in Goose Bay. If we had stayed long enough, we would have done more.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

That is one positive suggestion I can give the Government of Canada. They would help that region and bring new foreign dollars into the country.
The second thing the Government of Canada could do is to set up in northern Newfoundland and Labrador a northern fishery development corporation. The Minister of Justice very blithely says, "If nothing else is done, the Atlantic Accord will make up for everything". I suggest he tell that to people along the Labrador coast. That is absolute, utter nonsense. There will be no immediate pay-off to the people in that area.
What should happen is an improvement to fisheries conditions in that area. A northern fishery development corporation should be set up.
However, let me say what the Government did. We had set aside $15 million for the northern fisheries development corporation.
